routes.description: Establish Christian revelation as the necessary precondition for truth, logic, knowledge, induction, evidence, and reasonable belief in God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the Christian God supplies the required foundation for intelligibility and that denying this foundation leaves the con account unable to justify its own reasoning.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's truth and necessary epistemic role to the conclusion that belief in the Christian God is reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective truth and knowledge require conformity to an absolute divine mind.
Establish that logical absolutes reflect God's thinking and cannot be grounded by autonomous naturalistic cognition.
Establish divine revelation as a certainty-conferring source available to human knowers.
Establish that nonrevelatory attempts to justify induction depend circularly on induction itself.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Christian revelation from competing religious authorities through internal consistency tests.
Clarify that Christianity functions as the argument's starting precondition rather than as an inference from generic absolutes.

routes.description: Defend fallibilist, evidence-responsive inquiry as sufficient for reasonable belief while requiring support for Christianity's claimed epistemic necessity.
routes.successCriteria: Show that reasonableness does not require absolute certainty, that logic and experience support provisional knowledge, and that revelation and Christian exclusivity require independent demonstration.

motionBridge.description: Connect justified fallibilist inquiry and unmet theistic evidential burdens to withholding belief in God as presently unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Define reasonable belief by valid inference and supported premises rather than by absolute certainty.
Ground inquiry in logical absolutes, shared experience, and appropriately limited confidence without adding God.
Require demonstration that Christianity uniquely accounts for logic, truth, and knowledge rather than merely asserting it.
Require a reliable mechanism connecting purported divine revelation to accurate human knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend induction as probabilistic justification without recasting it as deductive certainty.
Use disagreement among religious claims to require a truth-tracking method for selecting among revelations.

sectionSelections.title: Reasonableness, truth, and the burden of belief
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue fixes the motion-level standard and determines whether truth itself establishes reasonable theistic belief or whether supported premises and valid inference remain necessary.

proSelections.proposition: Belief in God is reasonable because God exists, and believing a proposition that is true is reasonable.
Without divine revelation an atheist cannot know objective reality or truth, while everyone knows God exists and suppresses that knowledge.

conSelections.proposition: Reasonable belief requires a valid argument with adequately supported premises, whereas absolute knowledge or certainty is unnecessary for acting on beliefs.
Supernatural causation warrants belief only if a testable, reliable connection between religious claims or practices and observable results is established.

sectionSelections.title: Objective reality, certainty, and radical skepticism
sectionSelections.rationale: The competing accounts of access to reality determine whether uncertainty about ultimate reality defeats secular knowledge or permits inquiry from minimal fallibilist commitments.

proSelections.proposition: A case that presupposes truth cannot be justified by a worldview unable to know reality, because truth cannot be known unless one starts with God.
Truth conforms to the mind of God because differing human perceptions cannot independently establish objective reality or make anything knowably true.

conSelections.proposition: Because hard solipsism has no known ultimate solution, inquiry should begin with existence, reliable reason, and generally reliable experience rather than additionally presupposing God.
Human uncertainty does not entail God, because reality rather than a person's asserted certainty is the arbiter of truth and God's existence still requires evidence.

sectionSelections.title: The foundation and intelligibility of logic
sectionSelections.rationale: Accounting for logical absolutes is a central burden because both routes rely on logic while disputing whether its intelligibility requires the Christian God.

proSelections.proposition: If human reasoning consists only of biochemical reactions in evolved brains, it cannot account for objective logical necessity or truth.
Logical absolutes are accounted for because they reflect God's thinking and are known through divine revelation.

conSelections.proposition: Making God the foundation of logical absolutes is explanatorily insufficient unless both that account and its claimed exclusivity over all other worldviews are demonstrated.
Truth and knowledge can rest on logical absolutes and experienced reality, while Christianity's exclusive ability to account for those absolutes requires demonstration rather than assertion.

sectionSelections.title: Revelation, reliability, and rival religious claims
sectionSelections.rationale: The reliability and distinctiveness of Christian revelation govern whether it can bridge divine omniscience to human certainty and distinguish Christianity from competing authorities.

proSelections.proposition: Evidence is intelligible only when one begins with God, who can reveal himself so certainly that every person knows he exists despite contrary professions.
Islam cannot supply a rival ultimate revelation because the Quran affirms the Bible and the incorruptibility of God's words while conflicting with the Bible.

conSelections.proposition: Competing religions, denominations, and revelation claims provide no reliable method for determining which purported god or doctrine, if any, is true.
Even granting a perfect God, no mechanism has been demonstrated by which a fallible recipient obtains infallible revelation, and invoking God reproduces circular justification.

sectionSelections.title: Induction and the direction of the transcendental argument
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether probabilistic prediction can be rational without revelation and clarifies whether Christianity is established from shared premises or installed as the necessary starting point.

proSelections.proposition: Validating induction by appeal to its past success already employs induction and therefore makes the secular justification viciously circular.
The transcendental argument does not infer God from absolutes but begins with the Christian God as the necessary precondition for making any absolutes intelligible.

conSelections.proposition: Inductive expectations are rationally justified as probabilistic predictions from recurring experience without claiming that the future must reproduce the past exactly.
Presuppositionalism does not justify reasonable belief in God when it asserts Christian necessity, shifts the burden to alternatives, and treats certainty as establishing truth.
